data.title: Dowling–Degos disease — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dowling–Degos disease** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is Dowling–Degos disease (DDD)?**
- Rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis ('reticulate pigmented anomaly of the flexures') with progressive reticulate hyperpigmentation of flexures; genes — KRT5 (keratin 5), POFUT1, POGLUT1, PSENEN
- Onset usually 3rd–4th decade, slowly progressive

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Reticulate brown-black macules coalescing in axillae, groin, neck, inframammary, antecubital and intergluteal folds
- Comedo-like dark follicular papules on back and neck, pitted perioral acneiform scars; occasionally epidermoid cysts, hidradenitis suppurativa association, seborrhoeic keratosis-like papules

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Filiform (finger-like/antler-like) downward elongation of thin pigmented rete ridges from epidermis and follicular infundibula ('antler-like'), with pigment at the tips, horn cysts; no increase in melanocyte number
- Galli–Galli disease: same + suprabasal acantholysis

**Q4. Enumerate reticulate pigmentary disorders (PYQ: genetically determined pigmentary disorders).**
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural reticulate pigmentation, comedo-like pits — KRT5, POFUT1, POGLUT1)
- Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (dorsa of hands/feet, palmar pits — ADAM10)
- Galli–Galli disease (DDD with acantholysis)
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (Dohi — acral mottled hypo/hyper — ADAR1) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria
- Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (KRT14 — absent dermatoglyphics)
- Dyskeratosis congenita (reticulate pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia — telomere genes)
- Incontinentia pigmenti stage 3, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Haber syndrome, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (acquired)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acanthosis nigricans (velvety, no comedones), RAPK (acral), Galli–Galli, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, Haber syndrome (rosacea-like face + flexural DDD-like), frictional melanosis, Addison's
- Histology distinguishes from adenoid seborrhoeic keratosis (similar pattern)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Difficult; cosmetic concern: topical retinoids (adapalene/tretinoin), hydroquinone, azelaic acid, Er:YAG/ CO2 or Q-switched lasers, IPL (variable)
- Genetic counselling

**Q7. Describe Galli–Galli disease.**
- Acantholytic variant of DDD (KRT5 mutations) — clinically same reticulate pigmentation with itchy papules; histology shows suprabasal acantholysis without dyskeratosis — differentiate from Hailey–Hailey and Darier

**Q8. Describe the generalised DDD variant.**
- Reticulate pigmentation extends beyond flexures to trunk and limbs, with hypopigmented macules in some — overlaps with dyschromatosis universalis

**Q9. What genetic counselling applies?**
- Autosomal dominant with variable expressivity — 50% transmission; examine relatives (often undiagnosed mild cases)

**Q10. Laser and procedure options with evidence.**
- Er:YAG and CO2 ablative lasers — best reported improvement; Q-switched Nd:YAG and IPL — variable; recurrence common; topical adapalene/ tretinoin and azelaic acid modest; avoid friction and heat

**Q11. Explain why it may be misdiagnosed as AN.**
- Both cause flexural pigmentation in adults; DDD shows reticulate (net-like) small macules, comedo-like papules, pitted scars and family history, no velvety thickening, no insulin resistance; biopsy shows antler-like rete in DDD vs papillomatosis in AN

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. What is the relationship between DDD and hidradenitis suppurativa?**
- PSENEN (γ-secretase) and NCSTN mutations cause familial HS; PSENEN mutations can present with both DDD and HS — impaired Notch signalling links follicular occlusion and pigmentation abnormalities

**Q14. What is Haber syndrome?**
- Rosacea-like facial eruption (early onset) with keratotic papules and DDD-like reticulate flexural pigmentation — considered a variant of DDD

**Q15. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Irregular brown reticular network with dark-brown dots/ globules and comedo-like openings

## Quick spotter facts
- Flexural reticulate pigmentation + comedo-like papules + perioral pits — Dowling–Degos
- Antler-like rete ridges

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Reticulate pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
